front: Visual metaphor: an OS is like a toy shop manager. What three things does a toy shop manager do?
back:
• Directs operational resources: employees, parts and tools; which employee works on which order with which tools
  • Enforces working policies: fairness, safety, clean-up (e.g. how workers on two orders share a tool)
  • Mitigates the difficulty of complex tasks: makes the shop's operation simpler and more optimized

front: Visual metaphor: how does an OS 'direct operational resources' and 'mitigate the difficulty of complex tasks'?
back:
• Directs resources: it controls the use of the hardware (CPU, memory, peripheral devices such as disks and network cards) and decides how those resources are allocated to applications
  • Mitigates difficulty: it simplifies the view of the underlying hardware; applications interact with the OS via system calls and the OS takes care of the difficult tasks

front: Visual metaphor: what policies does an OS enforce, and give two examples of resource limits.
back: Fair access to shared resources, and limits on the maximum amount of a resource an application or process can use. Examples: the number of files that can be open per process; the thresholds that must be passed for some memory management daemons to kick in.

front: OS definition: where does the operating system sit in a computing system?
back: The operating system is the layer of software that sits between the hardware components and the higher level applications.

front: Name the hardware components of a computing system (per the note).
back:
• CPU
  • Physical memory
  • Network interfaces (Ethernet/Wifi card)
  • GPU
  • Storage devices (disk, SSD, flash drives [USB])

front: Why must hardware components be shared among applications?
back: Except in some very specific environments (certain embedded platforms or sensors), all hardware components get used by multiple applications at once. Even a single CPU has multiple cores, so one CPU has more than one processing element to hand out; a server may run a web server, database, and simulation at the same time; a phone runs a browser, Skype, Facebook and the phone-call app.

front: Is there a formal definition of an operating system? How does the lecture define it instead?
back: No single formal definition exists. The lecture builds its understanding from the role the OS serves and the functionality it must provide.

text: {{c1::Abstraction}} simplifies what the hardware looks like to the software above it; {{c2::arbitration}} manages and distributes the hardware among the applications competing for it.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

front: Abstraction example: how does the OS hide the complexity of storage devices?
back: It provides a higher level abstraction, the file, with operations like read and write that applications interact with.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

front: Abstraction example: how does the OS abstract the networking resource?
back: It abstracts the network as a socket, with operations to send and receive data over it.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

front: Give examples of hardware resources the OS manages (arbitration).
back: The OS allocates memory for applications, schedules them for execution on the CPU, and controls access of applications to the various devices in the system. Overall it is responsible for all types of resource allocation and resource management on behalf of the applications.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

text: {{c1::Protection}} means an application cannot read another application's data; {{c2::isolation}} means an application cannot overwrite another application's memory.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

front: How does the OS provide isolation and protection for co-running applications?
back: It ensures each can make adequate progress and they don't hurt one another: it allocates different parts of physical memory to different applications and ensures that, unless explicitly intended, applications don't access each other's memory.
source: Main Functions of an Operating System

front: OS definition: what privileged capability does an operating system have that applications do not?
back: It directly has privileged access to the underlying hardware and can manipulate its state; application software is not allowed to do that.

front: List the four properties in the operating system definition.
back:
• Has privileged access to hardware and can manipulate its state
  • Hides hardware complexity
  • Manages hardware on behalf of one or more applications according to predefined policies
  • Ensures applications are isolated and protected from one another

front: Components quiz: which of file editor, file system, device driver, cache memory, web browser, scheduler are likely OS components?
back:
OS components: file system, device driver, scheduler.
Not OS components: file editor, web browser, cache memory.

front: Components quiz: why are the file system, device driver and scheduler OS components?
back:
• File system: hides hardware complexity, exporting a file instead of a block of disk storage
  • Device driver: makes decisions about the usage of the hardware devices
  • Scheduler: distributes access to the CPU among all applications sharing the platform

front: Components quiz: why are the file editor and web browser not OS components?
back: They are applications that users interact with directly, and they are not directly involved in managing (have no direct control over) the underlying hardware.

front: Why is cache memory a tricky case for OS resource management?
back:
Both the OS and the application software use the cache for performance, but the OS does not directly manage it: the hardware manages the cache itself. That is why cache memory is not an OS component.
Beyond the lecture: the OS does control whether a mapping is cacheable and issues explicit flushes where correctness demands them, but no OS component manages the cache.

front: Abstraction or arbitration quiz: classify distributing memory between processes, supporting different types of speakers, and interchangeable access of hard disk or SSD.
back:
• Distributing memory between processes: arbitration (managing memory and how processes share it)
  • Supporting different speakers: abstraction
  • Interchangeable hard disk or SSD access: abstraction

front: What role does a device driver play in hardware abstraction (e.g. supporting different speakers)?
back: The device driver knows the details of the particular hardware element. That lets the OS control the device without knowing those details itself.

front: Why is interchangeable access to a hard disk or SSD an abstraction?
back: The OS's storage abstraction handles the different types of devices underneath and hides them from the applications.

front: OS examples: what environments may operating systems target, and which does the class focus on and why?
back: Desktop or server, embedded, and ultra high end machines like mainframes. The class focuses on desktop and embedded because they are the most common, and on recent, current operating systems.

front: OS examples: which operating systems target the desktop environment?
back:
• Microsoft Windows (well known since the early 1980s)
  • Unix-based systems: OS X, Linux

front: OS examples: which operating systems target the embedded environment?
back:
• Android
  • iOS
  • Symbian

front: OS examples: where did Unix originate, and how do OS X and Linux relate to it?
back: Unix originated at Bell Labs in the late 1960s. OS X extends the Unix BSD (Berkeley System Distribution) kernel. Linux is a Unix-like, open source system bundled with many popular software libraries, with many versions (Ubuntu, CentOS).

front: OS examples: what is Android, and which OS do the class's in-depth examples use?
back: Android is an embedded form of Linux. The class focuses on Linux: most illustrative, in-depth examples are based on it.

front: Which abstractions correspond to the applications the OS executes, and what mechanisms go with them?
back: The abstractions are process and thread. The mechanisms are create (launches an application so it starts executing) and schedule (makes it actually run on the CPU).

front: Which abstractions correspond to the hardware resources the OS manages?
back: File (storage device), socket (network card), and memory page (physical memory).

front: OS Elements: what do the mechanisms open, write, and allocate do?
back:
• open: gains access to a particular device or hardware component
  • write: updates its state
  • allocate: makes sure an application has access to that resource

front: What is a policy in OS terms, with an example?
back: A policy determines exactly how the mechanisms will be used to manage the hardware. Examples: the maximum number of sockets a process has access to, or which data is removed from physical memory, based on an algorithm like least-recently used (LRU).

front: Memory management example: what is a memory page and its typical size?
back: A memory page is an addressable region of memory of some fixed size, typically 4KB.

front: Memory management example: what do the mechanisms allocate and map do for a page?
back: allocate actually allocates the memory in DRAM; mapping maps the page into the address space of the process so the process can interact with the underlying DRAM.

front: Memory management example: what does the page abstraction hide from its users?
back: Over time the page may be moved to different places in memory or to disk; users of the page abstraction don't have to worry about those details. That is the point of the abstraction.

front: What is swapping?
back: Moving a page out of physical memory and onto disk.

front: Memory management: deciding when to move a page from DRAM to disk is an example of what, and what algorithm might implement it?
back: It is an example of a policy. One implementation uses the least-recently-used (LRU) algorithm, moving pages accessed longest ago onto disk.

front: OS design principle: what is 'separation of mechanism and policy'?
back: Incorporate flexible mechanisms that can support a number of different policies. For memory, one mechanism should generalize to LRU, LFU, and random.

front: What single mechanism can support the LRU, LFU, and random memory policies?
back: A mechanism that tracks how memory locations have been accessed (their frequency or last-touched time), or ignores that information entirely. Any one of the three policies can be built on top of it.

front: OS design principle: 'optimize for the common case' means considering what questions?
back:
• Where will the OS be used; what machine (how many CPUs, how much memory, what devices)?
  • What will the user want to execute?
  • What are the workload requirements and how does the workload actually behave?

front: How does optimizing for the common case relate to separating mechanism and policy?
back: The common case may change in different contexts. Understanding it helps the OS implement the correct policy, which relies on generalized mechanisms; in different settings, different policies make more sense.

front: What two execution modes do computer systems distinguish between?
back: Privileged kernel mode and unprivileged (user) mode.

front: In which mode does the OS run, and why? In which mode do applications run?
back: The OS runs in privileged kernel mode because it must have direct access to hardware. Applications generally run in unprivileged user mode.

front: OS protection boundary: where can hardware access be used, and what supports crossing from user mode to kernel mode?
back: Hardware access can only be utilized in kernel mode, from the OS directly. Crossing from user mode to kernel mode is supported by the hardware on most modern platforms.

front: How does hardware distinguish kernel mode from user mode at the instruction level?
back: In kernel mode a special bit is set in the CPU, and any instruction that directly manipulates hardware is permitted. In user mode that bit is not set and those instructions are forbidden.

front: What happens when a privileged instruction is encountered during non-privileged execution?
back: The application is trapped: its execution is interrupted and the hardware switches control to the OS at a specific location, where the OS checks what caused the trap.

front: After a trap, what can the OS decide to do?
back: It can decide whether to grant the access or potentially terminate the process.

front: What interface lets applications get privileged access to hardware resources?
back: The OS exposes an interface of system calls that the application can invoke.

front: Give three example system calls and the resource each targets.
back:
• open (file)
  • send (socket)
  • malloc (memory)

front: The lecture gives malloc as a memory system call. What is it strictly?
back: A C library function, not a system call. It gets memory from the kernel through the brk or mmap system calls.

front: What are signals in the OS protection context?
back: Signals are a way for the operating system to send notifications to the application.

front: System call flow: what is the sequence of control between process and OS?
back: A currently executing process needs hardware access, so it makes a system call (possibly passing arguments); control passes to the OS, which accesses the hardware; execution control and any necessary data are passed back to the application process.

front: System call flow: what mode transitions occur in terms of context switching?
back: A change from user mode to kernel mode to user mode.

front: Why isn't making a system call cheap?
back: It changes the execution context from the user process to the kernel, passes whatever arguments the operation needs, and jumps to the kernel-memory location holding that call's instruction sequence; the return does all of it in reverse, ending at the exact instruction where the call was made.

front: How can arguments be passed to a system call?
back: Either directly from process to OS, or indirectly by specifying their address.

front: What is synchronous mode for a system call?
back: The process waits until the system call completes. Asynchronous modes also exist.

front: What two steps must an application perform to make a system call?
back:
1. Write the arguments and save the relevant data at a well-defined location
  2. Make the call using a specific system call number

front: What does the kernel use the system call number for?
back: To work out how many arguments to expect and where to look for them.

front: Why are user/kernel transitions necessary during application execution?
back: An application may need to access some hardware, or request a change in the hardware resources allocated to it. Only the kernel may perform those operations; an application cannot change registers to give itself more CPU or memory.

front: Crossing the OS boundary: besides privileged instructions, what else causes a trap, and what bit does the hardware set?
back: A memory access for which the unprivileged application doesn't have permission. The hardware transfers control from the process to the OS and marks it by setting the special privilege bit.

front: Crossing the OS boundary: once a trap hands control to the OS, what determines whether the request is granted or denied?
back: The policies the OS supports.

front: Crossing the OS boundary: how long do the transition instructions take on a 2GHz Linux box?
Besides the transition instructions, what hidden cost does crossing the OS boundary impose?
back: The OS brings its needed content into the hardware cache, replacing the application's content. The application then pays for those evictions on subsequent accesses: cache access is a few cycles, but memory access can be hundreds of cycles.

front: OS services: name three services directly linked to hardware components and their component.
back:
• Scheduling component (CPU, or even multiple CPUs): controls access to the CPU
  • Memory manager (physical memory): allocates physical memory to co-running applications and makes sure they don't overwrite each other's memory
  • Block device driver (block device)

front: Give an example of an OS service that is a higher-level abstraction without a direct hardware component.
back: The filesystem as a service.

front: List the basic OS services.
back:
• Process management
  • File management
  • Device management
  • and so forth
All are made available to applications through system calls.

front: How do Windows and Unix compare in the system calls and abstractions they provide?
back: They are very different operating systems, but the types of system calls they provide and the abstractions around them line up closely. Both have process control (create, exit, wait), file creation, and so on.

front: System calls quiz: name four other Linux system calls from the quiz and what each does.
back:
• kill: sends a signal to a process
  • setgid: sets the group identity of a process
  • mount: mounts a file system
  • sysctl: reads or writes system parameters

front: The lecture links setgid16/setgid32 to 16/32 bit systems. What is the actual reason for the split?
back: The original call took a 16 bit group ID, and Linux 2.4 added a 32 bit version. The split is about the width of the group ID, not the word size of the machine.

front: What happened to sysctl after the lecture?
back: It was removed in Linux 5.5. System parameters are now read and written through the /proc/sys filesystem.

front: What characterizes a monolithic OS design?
back: Historically, operating systems have a monolithic design. Everything is included off the bat: every possible service any application could require or any hardware could demand is already part of the OS, e.g. several file systems at once (one for sequential workloads, another optimized for random I/O, common with databases). This makes the OS potentially very large.

front: Monolithic OS: pros?
back:
• Everything included: the abstractions and all the services are packaged at the same time
  • Compile-time optimizations (inlining, for example)

front: Monolithic OS: cons?
back:
• Too much state and too much code, which is hard to maintain, debug and upgrade
  • Large memory requirements (which can impact performance)

front: Which OS uses the modular design, and how prevalent is it?
back: Linux uses this design, and it is the dominant approach today.

front: How does a modular OS let you extend functionality?
back: It has a basic set of services and APIs; anything not included can be added as a module (e.g. which file system or scheduler the OS uses). The OS specifies an interface any module must implement, so you can swap the implementation behind it. Modules can be dynamically installed.

front: Modular OS: give the file-system example of why swappable modules matter.
back: Database applications accessing random offsets want a file system optimized for random access; a workload that streams through files start to finish wants one optimized for sequential access. Each application can interface in the way that makes most sense to it.

front: Modular OS: pros?
back:
• Easier to maintain and upgrade
  • Smaller footprint
  • Less resource needs

front: Modular OS: cons?
back:
• Modularity and indirection can reduce some optimization opportunities (typically not a significant performance impact)
  • Maintenance can still be an issue, as modules from different codebases can be slung together at runtime, and can be a source of bugs

front: Modular OS: how can its smaller code base improve performance?
back: A smaller code base is less resource intensive, leaving more memory for applications, which can lead to better performance.

front: What does a microkernel require at minimum?
back: Only the most basic OS primitives: an address space and a thread, which together are enough to represent an executing application and its context.

front: In a microkernel, where do file systems and device drivers run?
back: Outside the OS, at unprivileged user level.

front: Why is IPC a core abstraction and mechanism of a microkernel?
back: Because components like file systems and drivers now live in separate user-level processes, the setup requires lots of inter-process communication, so the microkernel supports IPC as a core abstraction and mechanism.

front: Microkernel: pros?
back:
• Size (lower overheads, better performance)
  • Verifiability (valuable where correct behavior is critical, like some embedded devices or certain control systems)

front: Microkernel: cons?
back:
• Bad portability (often customized to underlying hardware)
  • Harder to find common OS components due to specialized use case, leading to software complexity
  • Expensive cost of frequent user/kernel crossing

front: Linux architecture: list the layers from hardware up.
back:
1. Hardware
  2. Linux kernel
  3. Standard libraries (sys call interface)
  4. Utility programs (shells/compiler)
  5. User applications

front: What are the main logical components of the Linux kernel?
back:
• I/O management
  • Memory management
  • Process management
These components have well defined functionality, as well as interfaces; each subcomponent can be modified or replaced because of modularity.

front: Mac OS X architecture: what microkernel does it use and what does that microkernel handle?
back: The Mach microkernel, which handles memory management, thread scheduling, and IPC including remote procedure calls (RPC).

front: Mac OS X architecture: what does the BSD component provide?
back:
• Unix interoperability (via a BSD command line interface)
  • POSIX API support
  • Network I/O interface

front: Mac OS X architecture: what are the I/O kit and the kernel extension kit for?
back: The I/O kit is for device drivers; the kernel extension kit is for dynamic loading of kernel components.
